unit.title: The Tribunal's Own Architecture
unit.moc: files only state — hub CLI — lanes & family rule — which AI for which job — grounding = proof — how disagreements become decisions — state layout — claim ledger & map

checkpoint.title: Checkpoint 3 — gate (the core one)
checkpoint.prompt: Describe the whole machinery — fanout → convergence → verify → record — and where the claim ledger and the map sit in it.

facts.text: The tribunal keeps **files as the only state**. The AI session is disposable — when it ends, nothing about the tribunal is lost, because everything that matters lives as files in the repository, never in the model's memory.

Why files instead of a database or memory? Any session can be thrown away and rebuilt. There is no single-session dependency: a crashed or fresh process just re-reads the files from disk and keeps working, so nothing takes the whole system down with it.

Becoming the hub is pure file-reading: a fresh session reads **the blueprint document** and the ledger — that pair is the entire bootstrap. On 2026-08-12 a clean shell with zero inherited environment found `hub` and ran the whole loop from files alone.
A common mistake is treating the chat log or the model's memory as the state. Those vanish between sessions — if a fact isn't written to a file, the tribunal treats it as gone.

exercises.prompt: What is the tribunal's only state?
What does a fresh session need to read to become the hub?
options: a snapshot of the model weights

exercises.prompt: The clean-session bootstrap was proven on 2026-08-12 — a fresh shell with zero inherited env found `hub` and ran the whole loop from files alone.

facts.text: **`hub`** is the command-line tool that runs the tribunal. It fans a brief out to the lanes **blindly and in parallel**, collects their answers, and drives the whole sitting from the terminal.

Why a CLI? It makes the tribunal scriptable, re-runnable, and watchable without a UI. A self-rolled per-lane timeout watchdog — not GNU `timeout`, which macOS lacks — means no single slow lane can hang the whole run.

Running `hub run` fans the brief to the lanes in parallel; `hub verdict` and `hub gate` apply **gate-enforced** verdicts where `--force` is the human override. Other subcommands cover `eval`, `winrate`, `playbook`, `cost`, `moc`, `status`, and `log`.
A common mistake is thinking a verdict is just a vote tally. It isn't — the verdict is **gate-enforced**, and only a human `--force` can override the gate. The tool also keeps a ledger per Quorum.

exercises.prompt: What does `hub run` do?
options: blind + parallel fanout of the brief to the lanes

exercises.prompt: The watchdog is:
options: a self-rolled per-lane timeout watchdog, no GNU timeout needed

exercises.prompt: What enforces a verdict in `hub`?
options: gate-enforced verdicts, with `--force` as the human override

lessons.title: Model Lanes: Why We Use Different AIs (and Limit Same-Family)

facts.text: A **lane** is one AI model wired into the tribunal. The live inventory mixes families — `cc-fable` (Claude, strongest), DeepSeek flash/reasoning, `oc-qw` (local), `oc-or`/`oc-light` (nemotron), `oc-nim` (gpt-oss), and `crush-glm`.

The tribunal limits **same-family** lanes because they share correlated errors — two DeepSeek models tend to hallucinate the *same* wrong 'fact'. So the DeepSeek family (`cc-ds`, `oc-ds`, `cc-pro`, `oc-pro`) is counted **once** per sitting: pick only one.

In a real sitting you might run `cc-fable` + `oc-qw` + `oc-or` — but never two DeepSeek lanes together. Nemotron is capped at **2** (`oc-or`, `oc-light`), `oc-qw` stays local/private, and `oc-nim` is held back by a slow cold start.

A common mistake is assuming 'more lanes = smarter'. The lesson behind the family rule is **diversity**, not quantity: a panel of unrelated models beats a bigger panel of cousins. That is the tribunal's independence mechanic.

exercises.prompt: How many DeepSeek-family lanes may a sitting use?
The reason for the family rule is:
Match each lane family to its rule.

facts.text: **Routing** decides which lanes sit on a problem. The default panel is **2 lanes**; 4 lanes are reserved for high-stakes work only.

Why route by class? Routing matches the problem to the cheapest lane that can still be trusted. Cheap independent votes handle fact-checks (with `cc-fable` only to break ties), while reasoning-heavy work gets the stronger reasoning lanes plus a local check.
A code-debug sitting uses `oc-ds` + `oc-qw`; deep reasoning uses `oc-pro`/`cc-pro` + `oc-qw`. For **secrets or client data** the only allowed lane is `oc-qw` — it never leaves the machine.

A common mistake is assuming the strongest model (`cc-fable`) should always lead. It doesn't: it is held in reserve to break ties, and sensitive data is routed to the local lane regardless of strength.

lessons.title: Grounding = Proof from Your Repo + Fresh Docs

facts.text: **Grounding** means a verdict is backed by proof, not vibes. `sb` answers 'true in MY repos', fresh docs answer 'true TODAY', and lanes answer only 'generally true'.

Why ground every verdict? Without proof a verdict is just a confident guess. That is why every verdict must cite **at least one** of the first two sources — the repo or a fresh doc — so a reader can actually check the claim.

A lane that writes a verdict citing only another lane's opinion — with no `sb` chunk and no fetched doc — is a **grounding violation**. Real sittings down-grade to 'opinion' when there is nothing to cite.

A common mistake is treating a lane's agreement as proof. If there is no `sb` hit and no doc, the correct move is to **refuse or down-grade to opinion**, not to quote a fellow lane as if it were a source.

exercises.prompt: Every verdict must cite at least one of:
options: an `sb` chunk or a fresh doc

exercises.prompt: When there is no `sb` hit and no fetchable doc, the tribunal should:
Which of these is a GROUNDING violation?
exercises.scenario: A lane writes a verdict citing only another lane's opinion, with no `sb` chunk and no fresh doc.

facts.text: **Convergence** turns disagreement into a decision by decomposing claims into atoms and accepting each **only if a grounding source survives**. Agreement without a source is labeled 'probable, unverified'.

Why not just take the majority? Raw majority is **convergence theater**: same-family models hallucinate the same 'fact' together, so 3 of 4 lanes explicitly reject majority voting. Source-backed agreement is the only real signal.

When lanes clash, a **fresh** lane — armed with the evidence and rotated so Claude doesn't silently become ground truth — arbitrates. It is never the strongest lane by default, and never the first to finish.
A common mistake is reading '3 lanes agree' as 'verified'. Three agreeing lanes with no source are still 'probable, unverified'; the verifier's job is to find the source, not count heads.
In the game this is the **checkpoint**: the gate the player must pass is the tribunal's gate-enforced verdict — a claim only becomes 'verified' when a grounding source, not a headcount, backs it.

exercises.prompt: Majority agreement WITHOUT a source is labeled:
Why is majority alone "convergence theater"?
options: same-family models hallucinate the same "fact" together

exercises.prompt: The verifier role should be:
options: a fresh lane armed with the evidence, rotated

facts.text: Every sitting gets a folder holding three things: the **intake** file (the problem plus its success criteria), the **lanes** folder (raw outputs, one file per lane), and the **verdict** file (the converged answer).

Why split them? Keeping intake, raw lanes, and verdict separate makes each role auditable. Anyone can later read *what was asked*, *what each lane said*, and *what was decided* — without the session that produced it.
Alongside the folder, the global ledger gains **one line**: date, class, lanes used, winner, and cost. The verdict file itself records the converged answer plus **dissents and citations**.

A common mistake is thinking the ledger holds the full outputs. It doesn't — it is a single summary line; the raw lane outputs stay in the lanes folder, and the decision with its dissents stays in the verdict file.

lessons.title: The Claim Ledger: Every Decision Tracked. The Map: How It All Connects.

facts.text: The **claim ledger** is a structured table of every decision. Each record carries `claim_id`, `sitting`, `class`, `claim`, `source`, `support`, `contradiction`, `confidence`, `review_state`, `added`, and `reviewed`.

Why records instead of prose? Tracking claims as records turns 'we decided X' into something reviewable. `confidence` is one of `probable` | `verified` | `contested`, and a claim is `accepted` only after a real-data re-check, not on agreement alone.

The ledger is generated by `hub eval`, never hand-maintained. A real convergence sitting regenerates the **MoC** — a single Mermaid map whose nodes are sittings and whose edges are frontmatter links like `relates:` / `supersedes:` / `depends_on:`.
A common mistake is treating 'accepted' as 'everyone agreed'. It isn't — a claim is `accepted` only after **at least one** real-data re-check, regardless of how confident the sitting felt.
In the game, the claim ledger is the **XP ledger** — every verdict you earn is a tracked, reviewable record — and the MoC is the **path** (the map of contents) that connects each sitting to the next.

options: a Mermaid map of contents, nodes = sittings
